cim: Arizona company’s AI system keeping residents safe at senior living homes
cim_eredeti: Arizona company’s AI system keeping residents safe at senior living homes
szoveg_eredeti:
SURPRISE, AZ (AZFamily) — An artificial intelligence system recognized as a standout invention is helping prevent falls among residents in Arizona senior living communities.

The technology, called Paul and developed by the Scottsdale-based company Helpany, was recently named one of Time’s Best Inventions of 2026 in the medical and healthcare category.

The company has also rolled out ePaul, a new wearable device that looks like a fitness tracker.

“It’s a testament to our clients, because they are the ones using the technology, and changed the lives of the residents for the better,” said Sandro Cilurzo, co-founder and CEO of Helpany.

Paul is a radar-based device that uses artificial intelligence to analyze movement without cameras and microphones.

Cilurzo said he created Paul because he saw a need for a system that would protect privacy.

“How somebody takes their steps, gait, posture, stride length, how somebody sleeps and rests at night is highly predictive for underlying maybe unknown health challenges,” Cilurzo said.

Caregivers use a dashboard that alerts them to changes, while residents receive a daily health and wellness report.

“These residents can remain longer independent, and this was the whole goal since day one,” Cilurzo said.

The ePaul bracelet works with the Paul system to measure steps and track location.

Wendy Souders, the vice president of Fellowship Square in Surprise, said the results speak for themselves.

“We’ve seen 70% reduction in falls,” Souders said.

The technology is also catching health concerns before they become more serious.

Jami Van Gysel, chief operating officer for Christian Care, said the system helped a resident who was “very independent and thriving,” but had “started pulling back.”

“She looked at her health and wellness report and realized that she wasn’t sleeping. She made a doctor’s appointment, shared it with her doctor, and they discovered that she had had a medication change and this was a side effect of that,” Van Gysel said.

Barbara Conley, a resident at Fellowship Square, told Arizona’s Family that she was skeptical of the technology at first but has come to appreciate it.

“I’m not used to any of this AI. I’m still learning how to use my phone so it is new, and I am willing to go with the flow to see what happens. Maybe some people don’t, but I really, really like it,” Conley said.

As Helpany is working to expand its technology to more senior living communities, Cilurzo didn’t discount the possibility of future at-home use.

“It’s a possibility, absolutely,” he told On Your Side. “Just how the system is designed, the technology, we see a path down the line but we are really focused right now to bring it to the senior living communities.”
